These sonic windows shift with every listen, drifting and cascading with restless energy, layered vocal manipulations, and deeply infectious grooves. Broken downtempo rhythms weave through pockets of sound design that feel rugged, earthy, and constantly in motion. Multi-instrumentalist Sven Strohschnieder‘s alias thrives within this abundant landscape, and the liner notes aptly describe these excursions as “Balearic downtempo to 80s coded pastoral electronica forays and off to heavy thuds of quasi slowed electro.” We couldn’t agree more. The fertile grounds explored by Billion One feel fully charged, primed for lift-off. A wonderfully unhurried collection, Hi Cozy Paradise opens with flowing, beat-heavy echoes on “Shimmering Heights,” its irresistible groove taking shape from first moments as it eases listeners into this fourteen-track foray. Kaleidoscopic sonic layers continually expand and envelop, yet standout moments often arrive in concise bursts, none more satisfying than micro-funk gem “Sounds Like You,” where stacked vocal lines and synth flourishes recall those wonderfully warped vocal treatments Tobias Lilja has long mastered. Elsewhere, microscopic details and time-stretched voices inhabit technoid flutter on “The Practise Of Not Thinking,” while Clark-inspired brittleness defines “Void,” launching skyward with melodic precision and crystalline momentum. Closing pieces “Glue” and “Forms & Figures” circle back toward vintage Mouse on Mars-style acrobatics, full of playful glitch work and beautifully fractured distortion, all held together by finely threaded vocal fragments that quietly bind every groove with fluid cohesion. Hi Cozy Paradise is available on Woodland Creatures. [Bandcamp] Hi Cozy Paradise by Billion One

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Recorded live to capture the essence of the music with no aid other than the musicians' own skill, 'III' (2026), the third album by the eclectic Italian band Aether, offers over 40 minutes of a stimulating sonic experience that traverses different genres and eras, at times transcending earthly boundaries to venture down unfathomable astral paths.Groundbreaking and experimental elements that evoke the Crimson-esque style of the 1970s in the celestial 'Oort Cloud', with the subtle contribution of guest flutist Rosarita Crisafi; contemporary jazz-inspired passages in the otherworldly 'Vogon', featuring the theatrical sung narration of fellow guest Claudio Milano and Matteo Ravelli's unpolished drumming; and scenes of constant tension and unease in the intriguing 'Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres', driven by the keyboards and synthesizers of Andrea Ferrari and Andrea Serino and Ferrari's first major guitar solo on the album, demonstrate a work that does not resort to commercially accessible formulas to broaden the reach of its musical vision, but is instead sustained by its commitment to the avant-garde.And building on the gentle piano chords of 'La M'lancolie Du Petit Prince' and its unsettling electronic textures, the band leans towards a greater dose of improvisation and creative chaos, with the wandering pianos and percussion of the swelling, expansive 'Panta Rei', crowned by Ferrari's second, unbeatable guitar solo; and with the jazz-infused, progressive suite 'Swerve', which winds its way through labyrinthine psychedelic paths - the superb interplay between percussion and keyboards, underpinned by Andrea Grumelli's bass, is particularly noteworthy- until it coalesces and finds its way out in its final two minutes.The vast ramifications of wide-ranging progressive rock generate a broad and versatile palette of sonic possibilities that bands such as Aether incorporate and fuse into their musical offerings, and "III" is a very good example of this.3.5/4 stars

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — With Carlos, Ric, and Wilfredo Wilson, two of founding members of Mandrill, the band's return not only to recording but to its roots reminded me of Santana's 2016 comeback with Volume IV, where he recaptured the Woodstock sound. Here, that Brooklyn funk and soul is present as if no time had passed, anchored by Mark Rey's guitar and Eli Brueggemann's synthesizer; and just as "Tribute to Ali" evokes Santana, as one would expect, "Ape's Back in Town" features those backing vocals so characteristic of Funkadelic."Old Fashion Dance" draws from soul, reminiscent of the Isley Brothers, yet features a jazzy touch in the saxophone, which evokes Stan Getz; its deep tone, combined with the backing vocals, creates a truly unique texture. "Summer in the City," with its rock-infused salsa finale driven by the guitar, works really well, you could easily picture it in a 90s Brian De Palma film.With its guitar, flute, played by Carlos Wilson, and the orchestra, Children of the World reaches such a dimension that the piano crowns the piece, almost like a suite. Gift of Life features the contribution of Ron Carter on double bass, and the pulse of 1970s New York is present in the percussion, backing vocals, and organ; it goes beyond a mere exercise in nostalgia by introducing new elements, avoiding any hint of self-indulgence.Mandrill Got da Funk is both classic and modern; it reminds me of the funk of Ruben Rada and his band, Totem. The horn section featured throughout the album is the DC Horns, with Dave Yarborough on tenor sax, Leon Rawlings on trombone, and Kieron Irving on trumpet. It also includes a DJ, in the vein of DJ Logic working with Vernon Reid.There is room for the blues on Black Wings, along with three soul-infused versions of "Old Fashion Dance" to close out the �lbum, which features Roy Ayers as a guest vibraphonist on nearly every track; the strings, combined with the funk guitar, evoke the feeling of a summer rendezvous in New York City.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Since 2014, Crippled Black Phoenix have been hailed as the Pink Floyd of the new millennium, infused with Black Sabbath-esque heavy riffs. This 14th album?a work of dark, gothic rock?aims for intimacy, navigating the sonic territories of Swans, Godspeed You! Black Emperor, and Mogwai."One Man Wall of Death" opens with a cinematic sample, voiceover, and oppressive synths layered over delicate acoustic guitar notes; it builds into an apocalyptic post-metal crescendo before a cinematic outro gives way to "Ravenettes," which bursts in with the metallic sound of Killing Joke or Rogue Male. An energetic Belinda delivers a catchy, punky, and intense dark-wave vibe?a fresh sound for the band."Things Start Falling Apart" features Justin, with a sound reminiscent of The Cure and the immersive atmosphere of Archive; it balances sadness and hope, melancholy and a mantra-like anthem. Dark, post-rock dynamics create a sound dripping with creative melancholy; the finale shifts into "No Epitaph / The Precipice," where Ryan's crooner-style vocals flirt with Leonard Cohen and Nick Cave, accompanied by slide guitar and distant echoes of The Eagles. The journey begins with a long, spellbinding crescendo designed to evoke divine, intimate landscapes. A touch of classic Pink Floyd emerges as the guitar solo transitions from a dark ballad into a liberating escape. The "epitaph" isn't King Crimson-esque but heavy post-metal, featuring roaring vocals and frenetic synths, before segueing into "The Void"?a track defined by a somber, drifting feel and grounding notes. It shifts into space-rock mode: NASA-style vocals and Japan-esque synths plunge into a mantra-like atmosphere?like a Pythia in the smoke or Patti Smith on acid. A truly contemplative track."Hollow's End" brings a return to the "Ravenettes" style: punky, metallic sounds paired with dark vocals?a witch in a trance. A defeatist reverb on a deafening synth pad segues into "Dropout"?featuring a latent decrescendo, distorted sound, driving bass, and a mantra-like vocal worthy of Anna von Hausswolff?while a tribal pad leads into "Vampire Grave," complete with a canine sample. A laughing, mocking voice casts a spell, plunging the listener into a post-punk sound reminiscent of Killing Joke and Billy Idol. The Floydian spirit is long gone, replaced by screaming guitars, heavy drums, and a head-nodding groove. The finale is epic?evoking Rogue Male through its dissonance and Ryan's primal scream."Colder and Colder" plays out as a melancholic love song, featuring a tearful synth and vocals from the *other* Justin that flirt with metallic dark wave. "Under the Eye" sees the return of Belinda?channeling the spirit of Patti Smith?set against a solemn piano. Melancholic tenderness and an entrancing atmosphere build toward a cinematic, Eastern-inspired contemplation. "Tired to the Bone" closes the album with a melancholic lament?a lullaby for an insomniac vampire. There is a hint of Portishead in this dark mantra. "Beautiful Destroyer" features a repetitive, cinematic vocal sample over a heavy, abrasive rhythm, blending distortion with ethereal flourishes from Tibetan singing bowls.Crippled Black Phoenix speaks of chronic exhaustion, grief, and the schizoid institutions that drive people to burnout and dissociation. Their sound is repetitive and metronomic, building through crescendos into complex experimentation that ranges from dark wave to icy, heavy space rock.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — With the release of an album as excellent as 2019's 'Family', US prog act Jolly can certainly callthemselves 'The Incredible' without a single ounce of exaggeration. All puns aside, this album isone of the most coherent and representative releases of this group, and being their fourth studiooffering overall, it exhibits a mature and focused sound that can easily be categorized as art rockwith elements of alternative, pop, heavy prog, and indie. For me, this is one of the truly great andunderrated prog bands of the 2010s capable of writing tremendous pop tunes! The refined andaccessible songwriting of Jolly is complemented by an array of heavy guitars and generouslytechnical riffs, as the band reminisces both Muse and Porcupine Tree in their prime years, but witha touch of pop-sided melancholy. The vocals of frontman Anadale are quite fabulous on this entirealbum, which makes 'Family' even more pleasing.Kicking off their set here is the song 'Lie to Me', which is a staggering prog number with somechunky guitars and a top-tier chorus that is definitely deserving of some major radio stationcoverage. Right from the start this album impresses with a solid modern production and a dense,vital rock sound that is as appealing as anything Devin Townsend has recently released. The song'Lazarus' comes next, which is another piece of pure Jolly excellence, this time with a spaceyelectronic sound in the background, capturing their more experimental side perfectly. Third track'Rain' is a mellow keyboard-driven song that slows the record down, while 'Ava' happens to be yetanother highlight - a funky contemporary pop song with metal instrumentation. Definitely an unusualbut charming entry. Another tremendous composition from this record is the intense 10-minute opus'Let Go', which is a complex and graceful piece of heavy prog. The final tracks on this album arereally strong, too, and I have to admit that I enjoyed both the moodier and the more dynamic songsappearing on this album. The entire thing clocks in at fifty-two minutes, and with all the peculiartwists and stylistic richness, 'Family' is a fun, enjoyable, and emotionally-loaded pop-prog albumfrom one of the genre's most understudied acts.Side note: the deluxe edition features a 25-minute bonus disc, which basically complements the mainalbum with three new songs and alternative versions of 'Ava' and 'Let Go', and happens to be a niceaddition to the main album, especially for the ones willing to dig a little deeper into this record.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Well, this debut release came literally out of the wild blue yonder, an unexpected gift from my homeland, a sprawling 88-minute tour de force that just may go down as the 2026 Prog surprise of the year. What makes this particularly unique, the band is from my hometown of Miskolc, so this has a personal connection that I cannot and will not dismiss. As per norm in Magyar prog, the talented crew is led by keyboardist/guitarist Jozsef Simko, a tight rhythm section featuring bassist Tibor Kozak and Gergely Sumalan holding down the percussive elements rather perfectly. Add two more special members, a petulant and active Peter Toth on electric guitars and a French expatriate who decided to live in Hungary, Madeline Besson, who sings in perfect English, having been in a band called Molly Moonshine . The production and sound are pristine , the cover wholly attractive and the entire set of songs perched on a delicate balance between technical savvy by the players, and an overt feeling of humility that goes a long way to seduce the prog listener. I felt an immediate sense of maturity within the grooves, a comfort zone that embalmed my space all the way through the 'hidden door' that leads into my soul.The nearly 10-minute opener "Stray Heart" certainly prepares the journey behind the hidden door with an ultra shimmering flurry of electronic serenity, building up into a more petulant variation that had ulterior motives in mind, as both rock riffs and classical movements meld into a platform for introducing Madeline's silky warble, setting the tempo. The harder section seamlessly blend in without to many ruffles , shoveled ahead by basalt bass and demonic drumbeats, the guilty guitars unafraid to use just the right amount of effects, flowing into ambient pools of synthy bliss, before letting the singer emote in a hushed vein. Its pretty and magically soothing."Release" features some of finest violin work heard in ages (Nora Kacsenyak), with mournful cello (Vivien Netti Novak) aching along for the ride, the strings swirling infinitely as if caught in a gentle gale, the piano splendiferous, and a relief of tension that is palpable. It's an accessible prog piece that suggests a liberation that cannot be avoided. An obvious reference to a dearly departed relative (Jozsef's father), becoming quite the eulogy in this case. The gorgeous piano work emphasizes a moment of loving reflection that is worthy of both attention and praise.The mood becomes a tad grimmer on the brooding "Rachel Revisited", a song about domestic abuse from the female viewpoint, an ominous commentary on the weakness of spirit that has poisoned the human condition since the dawn of time. Madeline does a masterful job on the microphone, her crystalline voice appropriately fragile, at times even trembling like a swollen lip. The instrumental presentation is dark and low-key, with progressive accoutrements, scratchy effects and doomsday symphonics that veer towards pain, the splintered guitars quietly shrieking in the front row. Impressive powerful.For a country famous for its thermal waters, as it sits in a massive underground aquafer, and yet has no access whatsoever to any ocean or sea, "Coastline" can only refer to Lake Balaton or the Danube River. The spotlight is a delightfully intimate saxophone solo (Peter Czako) that should put wind to many a sail, a common site on the Hungarian Sea as the Balaton is often referred to. Yet the theme chooses to describe the vagaries of human relationships, the perpetual roller coaster ride of control and miscommunication, suddenly challenged by loving laughter and tender moments.Then, the stylistics take a huge turn into even more progressive exercises , we land on a trio of megalithic epics. Clocking in a colossal 27 minutes and change, "The Brother of Sleep" stamps the prog seal of classification without any hint of hesitation. The inspiration emanates from Oscar Wilde's "The Happy Prince", a rollicking storyline that injects slick percussion, tinges of harpsichord and an airy opening introduction, before eventually turning the rhythm section into on propulsion mode, the vocal gymnastics breathtaking as they lead and harmony voices intertwine. Another gear is put into motion as the echoing chorus becomes escorted by a sweeping organ motif drawing 'silver ribbons'. The third section has a harder drum pattern to rely on, a metallic shroud in the arrangement that underlines a restrained instrumental prowess that paints quite the canvas. The brazen bass is lovingly up-front and center in determining the shifting sonic transmission, settling into an explosive symphonic climax. Very cool opus."The Other Side" wishes to convey a sense of universality, reminding us of the benefits of respecting cultural identities, not surprising in lieu of the unicity of the Magyar ethnicity. The handclaps underline a communal environment as if sitting around a campfire, singing songs, sharing stories and playing music. Can there be a finer panacea, and a better embodiment of peace ? I think not and know of none better!This four-part suite evokes the Book of Revelation, the quarter of an hour epic "Riders" closes the curtain on the now open door, with a wondrous sonic adventure, where light and darkness somehow dare to co-exist. There is little doubt that here the progressive elements really gallop along nicely, like the valiant horses on the Puszta plain, imagining whips cracking the air, and Puli dogs doing their magical herding. Jozsef's elegant piano exudes a prototypical Magyar melancholia, a heady cocktail often mixed with a hint of stubbornness, playful pride and profound emotional commitment. The Peter Toth guitar solo is an ideal example, genuinely sorrowful at first and then building up into a taciturn frenzy without going deliberately crazy. The ambient piano mid-section is drop-dead beautiful, the solitude broken by a lone bass elevation that alters the pace into a bluesy organ-led adventure where Madeline gets to sing her thoughts. The upward staircase of sound rises inexorably to its mighty conclusion, with a grandiose final section, majestic and imperious , reaching for the heavens , a magnificent pinnacle that seals the deal.One of the finer debut heard in many a moon, what really stands out is the utter humbleness expressed throughout ,and in our increasingly turbulent noise factory society, this has been quite a soothing experience that should bear many future releases in the future. Highly recommended with or without a glass of palinka.4.5 fractured coils

items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — 2025 brought the exciting news that Swedish female-fronted prog band Paatos had not only regrouped, but were ready to deliver a brand new studio work. `Timeloss', their debut from 2002, was a minor modern prog classic, effortlessly blending gloomy rock, weary jazz, hypnotic ambience and even glitching trip-hop and electronica. The departure of early guitarist Reine Fiske (finding success with alt-rockers Dungen) only slightly affected their sound, with the group retaining the sullen atmospheres but adopting more of an alternative rock/intelligent pop approach, even attracting to attention of modern prog notable Steven Wilson enough to work on their second album `Kallocain'.Thirteen years on from their last work, the same line-up since 2011's `Breathing' now offers `Ligament', and it shows the band continuing to experiment and break new ground, whilst also retaining all the subtle dynamics, melancholic moods, bursts of power and air of mystery that permeated all their previous works. Murky cinematic rock, wilting ballads, eerie distortions and freeform jams all blur together, and it even boasts a guest appearance from Mikael Akerfeldt of progressive-minded metal act Opeth.Launching to a cavalcade of Huxflux Nettermalm's breakneck drumming, opener `Chemical Escape' hits the ground running, all frantic energy and rattling bluster with a muscular chorus. Ulf Ivarsson's gorgeously murmuring, grooving bass (front and center the entire album) and Peter Nylander's shimmering guitars with grinding King Crimson-like reaching strains get mangled together, and while Petronella Nettermalm sighs and breathily coos "I'll be perfectly alright", the slinking and skittering electronic/drum-n-bass breakdown and stark violin scratches in the climax suggest overwise.The relentless `Beyond the Forest' is too up-tempo to be a traditional ballad, rather it's a darkly sultry duet between Petronella and Opeth's Mikael Akerfeldt that's full of longing...and a definite hint of danger. Wrapping around their voices is creaking cello and grand Mellotron rises, and the dark ambient outro ends on a very ambiguous note - is the piece about two lovers passionately pining for each-other, or is one of them trying to escape the dangerously obsessed other? You be the judge.Reflective and evocative ballad `I Deny' tiptoes with crystalline piano and ringing guitars that glisten with pristine beauty. Short but not even slightly sweet, the two-minute title-track is a breakneck runaway tantrum of noise, Petronella's voice a distorted snarl writhing around barb-wire guitars, and `Post War Liminal' is a lurching, stop-start staccato drone that wouldn't have sounded out of place on a Bass Communion album.Opening to weeping Mellotron veils, `I'm Letting Go' is a powerful yet reflective indie pop-rocker that soars with hope thanks to Petronella's defiant and rousing vocal. While her spectral voice looms and soars around `Who Am I', it's hard to relax with how `off' in parts the piece sounds, crumbling into the embers of a jazz-fusion improvisation, all scratching and scraping distortion, abrasive effects, ghostly and discordant piano and grumbling guitar trembles before its equally uneasy ambient close.`November' is a reflective lament around the gentlest of jazz patterings and lowly cavernous reverberations. But siren calls and angelic harmonies are quickly ripped to shreds with the violent `Last Ones of Our Kind', a raging political attack that ripples with danger and breathless tension. Patronella warns there's "no redemption to the found", and while offering one of the more overtly obvious and striking chorus moments of the disc, the band whips up a suitably stormy noise with multiple improvised passages of wavering keyboard swirls, crushing drums and blistering guitar salvos, sounding not unlike moments of Steven Wilson's solo works.Lurking closer `Svart' presses down heavy on the listener and refuses to remove its boot, a mucky gothic dirge that, despite the most minuscule glimpses of hope and respite, grumbles with a Magma/Zuehl-like oppression with its pounding percussion and dingy gulping bass. What, you thought with lyrics like the "Nothing will remain, nothing with live..." that the band would end on smiles and sunshine?!With this latest work, the band achieves a near-perfect balance of new directions and expected intense atmospheres that are still instantly recognisable as Paatos, but they are now not afraid to unsettle or move away from the more melodic, tune-based material of several of their last few releases. Petronella's voice has never been so powerful, and the instrumental interplay from the fellas has never moved so seamlessly from complex to subtle. It means `Ligament' is their darkest, most daring and experimental release yet, and certainly their strongest and most exciting effort since their debut.Welcome back, Paatos - four stars.(please note - `Port War Liminal' and `November' seem to be sadly absent from the LP release)

items.body: I Ya Toyah, the Chicago industrial artist, released the single “Apology” on June 26, 2026 through her own Femme Fatale Records. The I Ya Toyah “Apology” single arrives with an official video and follows “FEELINGS”, issued in May 2026. On “Apology”, I Ya Toyah sets heavy guitar riffs and pulsing industrial rhythms under up-front vocals, with piano passages cutting through, working across industrial, rock, electronic and alternative elements. She wrote and composed the track, Johnny K mixed and produced it, and Howie Weinberg mastered it. Apology by I Ya Toyah I Ya Toyah’s ‘Apology’ single and video The track turns on a repeated line, “Everyone owes me an apology”, and frames what its press release calls “a deeply uncomfortable question: when does justified pain become entitlement?” The lyric moves between accusation and confession and leaves the narrator’s motive, self-worth or superiority, unresolved. The video for “Apology” stages the song in an industrial realm built around a steel throne, with I Ya Toyah as a central figure and followers in ritual scenes. The release describes it as drawing on “industrial, gothic, and fetish-inspired visual traditions” and using theatrical symbolism rather than literal storytelling. “Apology” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp and through streaming services. I Ya Toyah previewed the song on her recent European dates before its release. About I Ya Toyah I Ya Toyah is the project of Ania Tarnowska, a musician, composer and producer based in Chicago, USA, born in Łódź, Poland, in 1980. Spoken in Polish, “I Ya Toyah” means “it’s just me”. She trained in classical guitar, piano and voice as a child, moved to the United States as a young adult, and graduated from SAE Institute in 2016 in music business and audio engineering. She runs her own label, Femme Fatale Records. She began the solo project in 2017 and released her debut album “Code Blue” independently on October 26, 2018, the same year as the single “Farewell – Mirrors Don’t Lie“, whose video premiered on Side-Line. In 2019 she joined the post-industrial group The Joy Thieves and toured with Pigface. A remix double album, “Code Blue Reloaded”, and the bonus set “Code Blue Revelations” followed in 2020, with the five-part EP “Out of Order” in 2021 and the acoustic EP “Ghosts” in 2022. In 2023 she released “Panic Room”, produced with Walter Flakus of Stabbing Westward, and opened US dates for that band. The work with Flakus continued on the “I am the Fire” EP and the album “DRAMA“, both released in 2024, the year she also toured the United States with Orgy and Cold and made her first European tour supporting Front Line Assembly. Side-Line covered her 2024 video for “Fraud“. After the May 2026 release “FEELINGS”, “Apology” continues her run of 2026 singles.

It serves as a deeply committed and critical reflection on the ongoing war in Ukraine. Musically and in terms of influences, many of the same elements from the album are present. The German duo continues to explore Industrial and D’n’B structures, but also ventures into quieter realms such as Ambient. Along the way, we encounter beautiful string arrangements, and later the journey shifts toward IDM territory. The EP offers a perfect blend of new tracks and remixes—one of which is by Ukrainian artist Kotra, also known as the head of the minimalist yet excellent label I Shall Sing Until My Land Is Free. EPs often feel more varied than albums, and that’s certainly true of “Belt To Blender”. It adds a rich, complementary layer to their now ‘older’ album, offering both continuity and something refreshingly new. (Rating:7½). items.body: Hybryds remains an extremely active project that released its first production 40 years ago. Throughout the years, Sandy Nijs, aka Magthea, has remained the driving force behind this Belgian pride, collaborating with a wide range of artists. At the end of last year, this new album was released, once again featuring collaborations with Peter De Koning, aka TraumaSutra, and vocalists Madeline Arndt and Katharina G. “Desert Of White Salt” takes us on a two-hour sonic journey, spanning a total of 14 tracks. The first part of the album in particular sounds brilliant. Hybryds naturally remains a reference point in Ritual music, but listeners will also recognize other influences such as Industrial textures and Trance-like fragments. The rhythms, combined with dark, repetitive soundscapes and Ethereal voices, create a hypnotic sensation, as if Hybryds aims to draw the listener closer to illusory gods. The whole work is perfectly constructed, with a true sense of harmony between all its elements. The second part of the album sometimes feels slower and less driving, but it still contains several standout tracks, including the more than 20-minute-long “I Walk The Wasteland”. This piece is a gem in terms of sound design, effects, and dark atmosphere. Both musical visionaries behind the project are perfectly attuned to one another, complementing each other down to the finest details. “Desert Of White Salt” strikes me as an ambitious work, as it is no easy task to keep the listener engaged for two full hours. Even so, in my view, they succeed in doing so on several key passages once again. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Drums Of Exile”: https://hybrydsmusic.bandcamp.com/track/drums-of-exile

items.body: Sam Rosenthal, founder of Projekt Records and the band Black Tape For A Blue Girl, has released “The Width of Shadows”, a solo album of electronic-ambient-drone music. The record is out now as a name-your-price download on Bandcamp and runs eight tracks across about 49 minutes. It is Rosenthal’s first solo ambient-drone album since 2015’s “As Lonely As Dave Bowman: Monolith.” “The Width of Shadows” collects eight tracks: “Sunflow,” “Flare Equilibrium,” “The Visitor,” “Solar Silent Sound,” “Filament,” “Angular Momentum, Vaulted Sky,” “The Width of Shadows” and the seventeen-minute closer “Orbital Equilibrium.” It is anchored by two older pieces – the opener “Sunflow” from 2024 and the title track, which dates to 2002 – with the rest built from unfinished recordings made over the previous five years and reworked with new synth textures. Rosenthal described his method in terms drawn from painting, saying the music combines “the spontaneity and gestural brushwork of Action, and the contemplative yet emotional drone of Color Field.” The Width of Shadows by Sam Rosenthal The album returns Rosenthal to solo ambient work after several years tied to Black Tape For A Blue Girl. Projekt reissued that band’s “Mesmerized by the Sirens” on vinyl and double CD, prepared a 30th-anniversary edition of “Remnants of a deeper purity” in 2026, and revisited his ambient past on the remastered 1992 collaboration “Terrace of Memories” with vidnaObmana. About Sam Rosenthal Sam Rosenthal is an American musician and the founder of Projekt Records, which he started in 1983 as a cassette label in South Florida. In 1986 he formed Black Tape For A Blue Girl, a darkwave and ethereal project whose debut album “The Rope” appeared on Projekt the same year; the band has continued for four decades through albums including “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” (1996), “As One Aflame Laid Bare by Desire” (1999) and “The Cleft Serpent” (2021). Rosenthal moved the label from Florida to Chicago, New York and, in 2013, to Portland, Oregon, where he is now based. Alongside the band he has released solo ambient and drone music, among it “As Lonely As Dave Bowman: Monolith” (2015); “The Width of Shadows” is his first solo album of new ambient-drone material since.

items.body: For more than three decades, Ataraxia has been regarded as both a household name and a cult act within the broad realms of Ethereal, Neo-Classical, Folk, and related musical genres. Throughout the years, Ataraxia’s core members – Francesca Nicoli, Vittorio Vandelli, and Giovanni Pagliari – have remained driven by an inexhaustible source of inspiration, deeply rooted in their spiritual experience. Of course, their remarkable talent plays a vital role, but so does the authenticity that consistently shines through in their compositions. Ataraxia offers a genuine remedy – perhaps even an antidote – to a world that rushes by like a bullet train. Ataraxia embodies reflection and wisdom, a profound love of nature, and a deep respect for ancient traditions, legends, and myths. With their latest album, “Sylfaera The Fair”, released through the Greek label The Circle Music and serving as the concluding chapter of a new trilogy, Ataraxia once again affirm not only their artistic brilliance but also the sincerity and integrity that define their approach to music. For me, Ataraxia’s “Sylfaera The Fair” is a truly immersive experience – one in which spirituality and artistry become inseparable. I had the pleasure of discussing the album and much more with Francesca Nicoli. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Ataraxia interview Q: Ataraxia was formed almost 40 years ago, and your latest album marks the thirtieth full-length release in this impressive journey. How do you look back on the young artists you were in the 1980s, and what has remained the common thread throughout this long career? Francesca: The first Ataraxia album was born in 1990, 36 years ago. We cannot describe a thirty-six-year process because we are always looking toward the so-called future; we are always looking ahead to what we will do. It has been such a fast, intense, and prolific flow that we are unable to find descriptive phrases that allow us to reflect on the complete body of work, because this is nothing other than the complete work of our life brought into music. We remember the experiences and enthusiasm of concerts around the world, the recording of the albums, but our emotions and vision are all directed toward what will be. Perhaps one day, a listener will be able to outline the path; we are the same people who have lived thirty different lives, so by necessity, we are others while maintaining that original root. It is as if we had been reincarnated 30 times in different bodies while maintaining the same soul that discovers new possibilities every time. Q: “Sylfaera The Fair” is the final part of an Ataraxia trilogy preceded by “Pomegranate” (2022) and “Centaurea” (2024). Did you know from the very beginning that it was going to be a trilogy, or did this happen more along the way? And what does this final opus represent, and how should listeners approach the trilogy as a whole? Francesca: We didn’t know it for sure, but we felt it; we knew it would end this way because we have always worked in trilogies throughout our career. It represents a part of our life in a mythological key, and therefore accessible to all and useful to everyone, like any form of art, to sublimate the meaning of existence for those who listen to it. The right approach is simply to listen to it in order, or even in reverse—from the third album to the first—and let the images that accompany the listening bloom, take the journey, enjoy the journey, and see how one comes out transformed by all this. A musical listening is always a journey, and from no journey nobody returns the same and to the same place. Q: Trilogies originated in antiquity, and I remain fascinated by how this format continues to evolve today. What fascinates you personally about the trilogy form, the symbols (like the number 9 in this album) in it and are there any examples from the wider art world that have particularly inspired or moved you? Francesca: The number three is a peculiar number, the number of perfection and communication. Cycles are completed that start from one, which also corresponds to the sign of Aries, and therefore to birth, the initial force that brings life to bloom and utter its first cry. Then, two is the mirror; we are in front of another who reflects our essence—without which we would not know who we are—up to the completeness of three, which is communication and creation, because from the union of two is born; the son, or what is created; by the energy of the two, becoming something new. Needless to say, Tolkien has always inspired us, and Tolkien also worked with the trilogy. But there are also references in painting and an interesting numerological studies we did years ago. Nine is the maximum expression of three (3×3), and nine are the characters of the album who will find themselves energetically creating “Sylfaera The Fair”, the realm of music, beauty, and harmony. Nine is the Hermit of the Tarot, the one who in solitude carries the lamp of knowledge on a path backwards, walking toward the past, in retrocausality. Then we have the Tesla sequence 3-6-9, which is a complement of mathematical and philosophical awareness that has always fascinated us. Q: I believe it is fair to say that mysticism has always played a central role in Ataraxia‘s musical universe and that it also reflects something about the people behind the artists. How important is the mystical dimension in your daily lives, and how do you perceive mysticism in the contemporary Western world, where it seems to be gradually disappearing? Francesca: We were born with this mystical nature, and since we were children, we have lived experiences linked to subtle worlds, amplified by life in medieval villages or on the Apennines of our region. Woods, rivers, mountains, and undoubtedly our numerous experiences on the Greek islands, as well as those on the Italian peaks, have created the substrate—the most powerful means—to experience our music in a mystical state. The mystical dimension in everyday life is still our nature; it is not a specific moment we dedicate ourselves to, it is the very way in which we perceive life and our experiences. We struggle to give you explanations regarding the disappearance of mysticism in the contemporary Western world because we live things from the inside; we exist in this dimension 24 hours a day, and this is our lens. In a certain way, staying within this dimension protects us—otherwise, we would not be able to write music, to feel in a certain way, or to imagine a profound bond between everything and between this and other possible dimensions. For us, mysticism is nothing more than feeling a profound connection, at both a cellular level and a higher mental level, to the heart of things, to the heart of a greater design that gives meaning to this earthly experience. A profound sensitivity is necessary, which can be wounded by the prosaic nature of life, and we must take care of it every day. Q: Ataraxia’s music often evokes ancient civilizations, forgotten rituals, and a sacred experience of nature, an atmosphere strengthened by the use of traditional instruments. How essential is this approach to your artistic identity, and how do you view modern music culture and the rise of AI, which in some ways seems to represent its opposite? Francesca: The nature of our music is as you describe; this approach is essential to be able to express ourselves in an honest, authentic way, which can bring forth sincere suggestions. Our creativity is indomitable, so we do not need ‘external intelligences’; due to a lack of inspiration; furthermore, we have been in the musical world for so many years that we feel no need for it at all. We like working with new sounds (natural and synthesized), but not delegating. We like having the responsibility for what we do, being the conductors of the orchestra, and using and refining our musical intelligence in order to remain operative and lucid. We don’t set ourselves against something; we act creatively to create something. Q: Speaking of traditional instruments, “Sylfaera The Fair” is once again an absolute masterpiece and a true tour de force, featuring contributions from guest musicians. How do you bring such an ambitious undertaking to life, and what does the composition process look like in practice? Francesca: For us, it is completely natural because every time, fellow musician friends arrive who integrate into the new project and the new album in a completely spontaneous way, and everything flows. We don’t have to tell them what to do or what not to do; they intuit it perfectly and create their melodies, blending their musical experience with our suggestions. Then, we work with great concentration on the rhythmic parts because we create them ourselves; these create the earth upon which the air and the water of the instruments move, and the fire—the Flame—is the union of all these forces in harmony, working toward a single goal: the creation of the specific dimension of this musical micro-universe that’s the album. Q: Were there any specific innovations or evolutions in the choice of instruments or in the overall production process during the creation of this trilogy and especially the latest album? Francesca: The first album of the trilogy, “Pomegranate”, utilized the simplicity of our essential instruments: classical and electric guitar, keyboards, cello, and voice, with few rhythmic patterns. It was an essential and poetic album. The second album of the trilogy, “Centaurea”, became enriched with more complex arrangements while maintaining the same instruments, to which drum patterns of a certain importance were added, varying the musical suggestions as we explored different genres (Folk ballads, Neo-Classical arias, more symphonic tracks, Dream-Pop, etc.). The new album focuses on a first part more closely linked to Nordic and Mediterranean Folk, introducing uilleann pipes, bodhrán, flutes, massive tribal percussion, and choirs, while the second part is more in line with our previous releases. Q: After releasing 30 Ataraxia albums, I wonder whether there are still artists or records that continue to inspire you. More broadly, what do inspiration and creativity mean when you have devoted so many years to the same artistic project? How have these concepts evolved for you over time, and how do you continue to nurture them? Francesca: Certainly, there are artists who inspire us greatly; they don’t directly inspire our music, but rather our soul. We are always listening to new music that we discover along the way, and music remains the soundtrack of our emotions. Since we were children, we have experienced creativity as a form of expression, as the natural nourishment of our own existences, and so now we are that expression—it is our DNA. Music is our language, our universe, our way of communicating with ourselves and with what surrounds us. Everything has evolved along with our life experiences, our maturity, our spiritual search, our sufferings, and our discoveries. We nourish it simply by living and experiencing the universe of life. Q: Glossolalia, or the use of imaginary language, has long played a role in your work and seems to fit naturally within the spiritual dimension of Ataraxia. How do you approach this practice creatively? Does it require a particular form of introspection, meditation, or discipline, and have you noticed an evolution in this aspect of your work over the years? Francesca: I have always used different ancient and modern languages in my lyrics, and there has always been a track in glossolalia on every album. Each language I used was chosen for the peculiarity of its sound, which suited that specific piece of music, and from there, the step to glossolalia is a short one. Usually, I listen to the compositions the band proposes and instinctively work on the vocal melodies, which already have a specific color connected to particular sounds. It is like a meditative process: I close my eyes, listen, and the sounds come out one after the other without any particular construction—they emerge spontaneously. It seems like a magical process; in reality, the voice becomes like a musical instrument that produces sounds articulated into words. The technique has been the same since the beginning, only in this latest album it was used much more extensively compared to the previous ones. Q: What are the current short-term plans for Ataraxia, and what can we expect from the band in the longer term? Francesca: In the short term, we are working on the live performance of this album experience—each time different, each time linked to the venue and the situation in which we will be performing. In the long term, we do not know yet. Everything is revealed to us along the path, just like breathing: we inhale, just as when releasing an album, we inhale to recharge with oxygen, which will allow us to exhale a new opus once again. About Ataraxia Ataraxia is a neoclassical dark wave and dark folk band from Modena and Reggio Emilia in northern Italy. The group was founded in the second half of the 1980s by vocalist Francesca Nicoli and guitarist Michele Urbano, with the line-up stabilising around Nicoli, guitarist and composer Vittorio Vandelli, and keyboardist Giovanni Pagliari in the early 1990s. Their work combines electronic technology with archaic and acoustic instruments, and their lyrics frequently reference nature, ancient cultures and mythological themes, often performed in historically resonant locations. In their first years Ataraxia issued self-released recordings such as “Prophetia” and “Nosce Te Ipsum” before working with labels including Energeia and Cruel Moon International, gradually building an extensive discography across cassette, CD and vinyl formats. Late-1990s albums such as “Historiae” explored medieval and liturgical atmospheres; the album was later issued by Ark Records and documented both studio and live recordings, including material captured in a medieval court in 1998. During the 2000s the band continued to refine its blend of neoclassical, ethereal and folk-influenced material on releases like “Suenos” and “Os Cavaleiros do Templo,” with several titles later revisited. Twilight Records reissued long-deleted works including “Saphir” and “Os Cavaleiros do Templo.” In 2016 Ataraxia released “Deep Blue Firmament” via Sleaszy Rider Records. Subsequent full-lengths included “Synchronicity Embraced” (2018) and “Quasar” (stylised as “ΘUASAR”). The collaboration with The Circle Music began with the 28th studio album “Pomegranate (The Chant of the Elementals)”, released in 2022 on digital, CD and vinyl formats. Ahead of that album the band issued several videos, including “Hlara Aralh” and “Aura Magi.” Pomegranate – The Chant Of The Elementals by Ataraxia Ataraxia’s 29th studio album “Centaurea” followed in 2024, again on The Circle Music in digital, CD and vinyl editions. Singles and videos from this period included “The Source,” “Galen,” “Viriditas,” “Coelestis” and “Ignis Pater.” Centaurea by Ataraxia And now there is the band’s 30th album “Sylfaera the Fair”.

Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi cite Front Line Assembly and Front 242 as touchstones. Alfa Matrix previewed “Chew The Loop” on its compilation “Sounds From The Matrix 026”, released on June 19, 2026. The EP ties its title to a stance against authoritarian rhetoric, fascism, war and prejudice, framing “every beat matters” as a call for awareness, resistance and unity; the campaign artwork carries the lines “Extremism has no place here” and “FCK NZS”. The label describes the record as turning “a simple message into a powerful call for awareness, resistance and unity.” The theme follows earlier Aesthetische records: the 2022 album “rvprty” was issued as a stand against far-right, anti-science and anti-democratic movements. About Aesthetische Aesthetische is the project of Brazilian musicians Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi, both previously in the electro-industrial act Aghast View. The duo formed this project in 2012 and have released through the Belgian label Alfa Matrix since their debut. Their albums include “Powerswitch” (2012), “HybridCore” (2014), “Co3xist3ns3” (2019) and “rvprty” (2022), alongside a run of EPs and singles. In recent years the duo released the EP “Confidence Is Silent” in 2024 and the EP “Selling Fear” in 2025, the latter also drawing on the legacy of Front Line Assembly and Front 242. Aesthetische have also discussed their approach with Side-Line in a 2024 interview. “Every Beat Matters”, released on June 26, 2026, extends the duo’s record of pairing club-focused EBM with anti-authoritarian themes.

items.body: LAHO, the Finnish dark electronic project of Konsta Vehkala, released the seven-track album “Death Machines” on June 26, 2026. The digital release gathers three of the project’s 2026 singles with four new tracks, among them a cover of Depeche Mode’s “Behind the Wheel”. LAHO blends industrial, EBM, futurepop and darkwave, with lyrics centred on dystopian themes and the darker side of human behaviour. Vehkala writes, programs and produces the project alone from Jyväskylä, Finland. “Death Machines” is the first LAHO album to feature vocals. Vehkala built the project’s earlier catalogue as instrumental work before resuming LAHO in 2024 after a 13-year break. The single “Programmed”, released on February 12, 2026, opened the new phase, followed by the singles “The Great Collapse” and “Last Rays of the Sun”. Death Machines by LAHO LAHO ‘Death Machines’ tracklist and the Depeche Mode cover “Death Machines” runs seven tracks: “Programmed”, “The Great Collapse”, “Cold New World”, “Decimated Memories”, “Fading Out”, “Last Rays of the Sun” and “Behind the Wheel”. The first, second and sixth tracks appeared earlier as standalone singles, while the other four are new to the album. The closing track reworks Depeche Mode’s “Behind the Wheel”, written by Martin L. Gore and first issued on the 1987 album “Music for the Masses”. Vehkala recorded, programmed and produced the album himself. He has tied the project’s lyrics to technology and modern life, describing the opening single “Programmed” as “a heavy hitting electronic track about our life in the ever-growing synthetic world.” The album is available digitally through Bandcamp. About LAHO LAHO is the solo project of Finnish musician and recording engineer Konsta Vehkala, based in Jyväskylä. It began in 2006 under the name Lahonnut Konkelo, a run of electronic and industrial experiments, with the name soon shortened to LAHO. The first EP, “The Other Side”, appeared in 2007 as a self-released CDr and was later reissued by the Italian netlabel Ekleipsi. Ekleipsi also issued the debut album “Escape from the Dying Star” in April 2009, a ten-track record made between 2007 and 2008 that mixed electro-industrial, synth work and distorted guitar. Vehkala followed it with the standalone track “The World in Flames” (2009), the single “Mechanigod” (2011) and the one-off digital release “Walking in the Air (1984 mix)” in December 2021. The project then went quiet for 13 years while Vehkala focused on other work. He resumed writing for LAHO in 2024 and added vocals as a permanent element, ending a previously instrumental catalogue. The 2026 singles “Programmed”, “The Great Collapse” and “Last Rays of the Sun” introduced the new direction. Alongside LAHO, Vehkala plays drums in the Finnish melodic metal band Psychework and has performed and recorded with Gian, Vipermilk and Lojohh, while contributing recording, mixing and mastering work to other Finnish acts. “Death Machines”, released on June 26, 2026, is the project’s first vocal-led album and its first full-length since 2009.

items.body: Teanga Teanga released the single “Around the World” worldwide on June 26, 2026. The project pairs New York art-pop artist Pamela Sue Mann with Dublin composer-producer Paul Murphy, who records as pxmurphy. Their version reworks “Around the World,” the 1956 standard, through synthesizers, electronics and strings rather than orchestral pop. Teanga Teanga rework a 1956 standard The single reinterprets “Around the World,” the title song from the 1956 film “Around the World in 80 Days.” Victor Young wrote the music and Harold Adamson the lyrics; Nat King Cole recorded a vocal version, one of several covers of the song. Teanga Teanga rebuild the track with cinematic synths, spectral textures, spoken passages and sweeping strings, with Mann on lead vocals. Murphy said the recording grew out of studio sessions and file-sharing between the two. “We suddenly got inspired by something,” he stated. “If we both buzz off it, we start digging in and seeing what comes out.” Mann described her approach to covering a standard: “If you’re going to do a cover, you’ve got to have something soulful — depth, honesty, empathy. Otherwise you’re just doing a cover.” The pair call the recording “time travel through music.” “Around the World” is available on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. The duo released an official video for “Around the World”, which streams on YouTube: About Teanga Teanga Teanga Teanga is the collaborative project of Pamela Sue Mann and Paul Murphy. Mann is a singer-songwriter, pianist, producer and poet based in New York and a graduate of Berklee College of Music. She released her self-titled album in 1999 and has recorded and toured with Suzanne Vega, Donna Lewis, Gerry Leonard and producer David Baron. Murphy, based in Dublin, co-founded Electric Penguins, whose debut album “Goodbye from the Electric Penguins” appeared in 2006. NPR featured the band, and BBC Radio London presenter Robert Elms named the single “Highgate Hill” his track of the year. Murphy also composes for television and advertising, and Electric Penguins released the album “The Way Lights a Fire” in June 2025. Mann and Murphy recorded “Around the World” remotely, the single now carrying their work forward under the Teanga Teanga name.

The Stars and the Underground “Echolocation” single features guest vocals from Hannah Berry of the Auckland dark-electronic project Talmar, and is the second single trailing the band’s forthcoming debut album “Guardians of the Night”. Stars and the Underground bring a sound that mixes post-punk, shoegaze and dark synth wave, with chiming guitars, low basslines and reverb-heavy vocals. John Mason handles vocals, guitars and bass, while John McDermott plays drums and produces. Echolocation by Stars and the Underground Stars and the Underground revisit ‘Echolocation’ with Talmar “Echolocation” is a reworked version of a song the band first issued on the limited “Evolution Circle EP” in 2019. For the 2026 single, the track was re-recorded with Hannah Berry of Talmar added on vocals. John McDermott recorded, mixed and mastered it at Arch Hill Studios in Auckland. The single follows “Lonely Black Hearts”, released on April 1, 2025, and both tracks point to the album “Guardians of the Night”. “While we have faced various challenges, I believe this has ultimately contributed to a stronger final product,” Mason stated. “‘Echolocation’ is a testament to this, as we initially introduced the concept in the limited release of the Evolution Circle EP. We chose to revisit the song, highlighting John McDermott’s exceptional drumming and production skills, along with Hannah’s enchanting contributions that elevate the track to new ethereal heights.” The video for “Echolocation” runs on the band’s official YouTube channel: About Stars and the Underground Stars and the Underground is a New Zealand project built around Auckland musician John Mason, who founded it in 2019. The current line-up pairs Mason on vocals, guitars and bass with John McDermott on drums and production; McDermott records the project at his Arch Hill Studios in Auckland. After a gap, the band returned on April 1, 2025 with the single “Lonely Black Hearts”, issued with remixes as the first single from the forthcoming debut album “Guardians of the Night”. “Echolocation”, released on May 22, 2026 with Hannah Berry of Talmar, is the second single drawn from that album. items.body: Based in Barcelona, SDH (Semiotics Department Of Heteronyms) released their third album this year, marking their first release on Artoffact Records. The album offers ten relatively short tracks that blend a variety of influences. One moment, the music leans toward Electro-Wave; the next, it adopts a harder, Body Pop-inspired edge. Elsewhere, the sound shifts into more Pop-oriented territory, occasionally even embracing Dance elements. As a result, there is plenty to explore and discover throughout the record. Adding to its appeal is the distinctive half-whispered vocal style of Andrea Pérez, which gives the songs an intimate and recognizable character. Every track has something interesting to offer, although I personally find myself most drawn to the harder-hitting compositions. Diversity is undoubtedly the album’s greatest strength, making it accessible to a broad-minded audience with varied musical tastes. My only criticism is that some of the songs feel a little too short, leaving me wanting more. Nevertheless, this remains a highly enjoyable release, filled with memorable moments and several standout tracks. (Rating:8).
